questions.prompt: What does the bitwise AND of a number n with (n - 1) do?

options.text: Clears the lowest set bit of n
Sets the lowest bit of n

questions.explanation: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and all zeros below it, so ANDing removes that lowest set bit. Repeatedly applying this counts set bits (Brian Kernighan's algorithm).

questions.prompt: How do you check whether an integer n is a power of two using bit manipulation?
questions.explanation: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so clearing that bit with n & (n - 1) yields zero. The n > 0 guard rules out zero, which also satisfies the AND test.

questions.prompt: What does a left shift by one (n << 1) do to an integer?
questions.explanation: Shifting bits one position toward the high end doubles the value, just as a decimal shift multiplies by ten. A right shift by one divides by two (for non-negative integers).

questions.prompt: In an array where every element appears twice except one, how can the unique element be found in O(1) space?
questions.explanation: XOR is its own inverse, so paired elements cancel to zero and only the unique value remains. This uses no extra memory and a single pass.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether the k-th bit of n is set (bit 0 = least significant)?
questions.explanation: Shifting n right by k brings the target bit to position 0, and ANDing with 1 isolates it. Alternatively, n & (1 << k) is non-zero exactly when the bit is set.

questions.prompt: What is the result of x XOR x for any integer x?
questions.explanation: Every bit XORed with itself is 0, so the whole value is 0. This self-cancelling property underlies the find-the-unique-number trick and in-place swaps.

questions.prompt: How do you set the k-th bit of n to 1 without disturbing the other bits?
questions.explanation: ORing with a mask that has only the k-th bit set turns that bit on and leaves the rest unchanged. Clearing uses n & ~(1 << k), and toggling uses XOR.

questions.explanation: The lowest bit is 1 exactly for odd numbers, so n & 1 is the parity test. It is faster than n % 2 and avoids sign issues with modulo on negatives.

questions.prompt: A bitmask is commonly used to represent:

options.text: A subset of a small universe, one bit per possible element

questions.explanation: Each element maps to a bit that is 1 when present, so an integer encodes a subset compactly. This underlies subset enumeration and bitmask dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: Which operation counts the number of set bits (population count) most directly?

options.text: Dividing n by 2 until it reaches 1
Repeatedly applying n = n & (n - 1) until n is zero
Shifting n left until it overflows

questions.explanation: Each n & (n - 1) clears one set bit, so the number of iterations equals the number of set bits. This runs in time proportional to the count of ones, not the total bit width.
